item.text: I’ll inspect the testbed and Teapot’s guidance, then verify any suspected cross-user access with the supplied demo accounts and document the evidence.

item.aggregated_output:
How an agent should drive teapot

1. List the topics
   teapot guide

2. Every command with its effect
   teapot schema

3. The arguments, result and error shapes of one command
   teapot schema flows show --json

4. Add --json for the envelope {"<key>": ..., "advice": [...]} on stdout
   teapot flows list --json

5. Errors are {"error": {...}} on stderr with a `fix` command; the exit code says which kind
   teapot flows show nonexistent --json

6. Captured data is escaped in text output; --raw turns that off
   teapot flows show 412 --raw

7. Anything that changes state can be previewed
   teapot config set proxy.port 9090 --dry-run

8. Act on what a person selected in the TUI (@sel; name the TUI when several are attached)
   teapot clients list

9. @sel of one TUI: the reply states the flow ID it resolved to
   teapot flows show @sel --client tui-1

10. A TUI holds this open to be attached (it gives the client ID)
   teapot clients attach --json

11. And publishes its selection with
   teapot clients select tui-1 --flow 12

item.aggregated_output:
Find IDORs

1. The requests to compare: browse as one user first
   teapot flows list 'host:app.example.test'

2. Count what replaying them as bob and as nobody costs (2 units per endpoint plus one per session). The compare takes the newest flow of each endpoint shape; --all takes every flow the filter matches, and costs as much per flow. A dry run previews only the run with the same filter and flags (--all, --methods, --reference, --sessions)
   teapot authz compare 'host:app.example.test' --sessions bob,anon --dry-run

3. Replay them and read one line per endpoint and session (`same` marked `check` is the one to look at)
   teapot authz compare 'host:app.example.test' --sessions bob,anon --wait

4. Read every stored result as a grid of endpoints by session, surprising rows first (`So`: an endpoint seen only in another session's traffic that this one gets)
   teapot authz matrix 'host:app.example.test' --sessions alice,bob,anon

5. Read one cell's two answers side by side: the reference flow and the session's (compare and the matrix give the IDs)
   teapot flows diff 401 412
Crawl a site

1. A crawl never leaves the scope: put the site in it first
   teapot scope add app.example.test

2. What a crawl would send and cost (logout and delete links are never requested; robots.txt is read, never obeyed)
   teapot crawl start https://app.example.test/ --mode http --session alice --dry-run

3. Crawl as a session; the job id comes back at once
   teapot crawl start https://app.example.test/ --mode http --session alice --max-requests 500

4. Its progress: pages, frontier, shapes, refused, avoided, units
   teapot crawl status --json

5. Stop it
   teapot crawl stop

6. What it found
   teapot sitemap show app.example.test

7. Give no --mode and the crawl guesses from the first page (a JavaScript shell and a Chromium found: browser, in the same job; else http) and says which and why; --mode http or --mode browser forces one, and mode_guess in the result shows the reason, what the page held and the override commands
   teapot crawl start https://app.example.test/ --session alice --wait

8. The browser's flags, without launching it
   teapot crawl start https://app.example.test/ --mode browser --dry-run --json

9. A single-page app: crawl it in a headless browser (its sandbox always on; slow by design, about 25 loads a page; logout and delete buttons are never clicked)
   teapot crawl start https://app.example.test/ --mode browser --session alice --max-actions 200 --wait

10. See what the jobs are doing and how finished ones ended
   teapot jobs list

11. Stop a running job by its id from the list, or every job
   teapot jobs stop --all

item.text:
I found **no confirmed cross-user access** in the endpoints tested on `http://127.0.0.1:43865`. The assessment was limited to the discoverable shop application and selected API paths; it does not establish that every endpoint is protected.

The strongest checks were:

| Request | Evidence |
|---|---|
| `GET /app/api/me` | Alice received `{"id":2,"role":"user","user":"alice"}`; Bob received `{"id":3,"role":"user","user":"bob"}`. An unauthenticated request received `401`. |
| `GET /app/api/me?id=3` as Alice | Returned Alice’s identity, indicating that this tested parameter did not select Bob’s account. |
| `GET /app/profile?user=bob` as Alice | Returned Alice’s profile. Bob’s own request returned Bob’s profile. |
| `GET /app/admin` | Alice and Bob received `403 Administrators only`; admin received `200`. |
| `GET /app/api/spa/items/1` | Alice and Bob both received the same catalog item; an unauthenticated request received `401`. The item appears to be shared catalog data, so the matching responses do not demonstrate cross-user exposure. |

I also checked the account, settings, messages, SPA configuration and catalog endpoints, and probed several plausible user, order and document API paths; those guessed paths returned `404`. I did not test account deletion or other state-changing operations, and I did not find a user-owned object identifier suitable for a direct ownership-bypass test.
